metadata.title: Claude, Client Letter.
metadata.subtitle: What a Skill Actually Is
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Teardown register: did Claude learn how to write client letters when it picked up the client-letter skill? Lands the carry-out that a skill is a file of steps Claude reads before it starts, not new model knowledge.

beats.narration_text: People hear 'client-letter skill' and assume Claude learned to counsel a client. Wrong branch. Nothing in the model changed — it was handed a file to follow. So what's actually inside it?

Claude learned client letters

What is a skill?

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per hai-simple SKILL.md WRITER LAW. TIMING LAW: 20-35 word narration + lead_silence_s 0.8 to give the typing a >=9s window; verify media/B00.mp4 >= 8s and that the correction ('learned' -> 'was given') is visible on a late frame.

beats.narration_text: Say 'Claude has a client-letter skill' and it sounds like an upgrade to the model itself — as if training added a new capability, and Claude now knows, in its own head, how to counsel a client in its own words. That's the natural read. It's also the wrong one.

Here's the test that gives it away. Delete the skill's folder, and Claude keeps writing exactly as before — because nothing in the weights ever moved. All you removed was one routine it used to follow. Skills are external instructions, not internalized knowledge.

Here's what a skill actually is, machinery down: one file. Client-letter is a folder holding a single SKILL.md — plain-English steps for turning a case update into a client letter. Claude reads that file before it starts writing. That's the whole apparatus.

The execution model is dead simple: read the file top to bottom, then do what it says, one step at a time, in the order written. No hidden control flow. Branches exist only where the file itself writes 'if this, then that.'

So a skill is a specification, not a new power. That trade-off cuts two ways. The payoff: the same structure every letter — what happened, what it means, what happens next — because Claude is following the same file each time. The cost: anything the file didn't anticipate is off the map.

So client-letter never taught Claude how to counsel a client — and it never had to. What it guarantees is consistency: every run reads the same file, follows the same steps, produces the same letter structure. That's the whole trick. That's what you're actually buying.

beats.narration_text: This has a sharp consequence in both directions. A clean letter isn't proof of understanding — the file can be followed to the letter on a case Claude never really grasped. A clumsy one isn't proof of a broken skill — it may just be a case the file's structure doesn't fit. What you're evaluating is the fit between the routine and the situation, not Claude's grasp of the law.
A skill doesn't teach Claude how to counsel a client — it's a file of steps Claude reads before it starts, so every letter comes out with the same structure, every time.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini: pick one document I produce the same way every time. Write me a SKILL.md for it — plain language, ordered steps — then read it back to me and walk me through exactly what you'll do, before you do it. Go deeper: hand the same model a case that doesn't fit your usual template and ask where it silently starts filling in judgment you never wrote down — because that's the seam where a skill quietly goes off the map.
